cleric.payoff: One nightly target and few result obligations make this simpler than Psychic. Genuine save feedback can build credibility; a quiet target list supplies little independent proof.
cleric.exposure: You promise Powerful Defense without necessarily supplying it. Claimed saves, movement checks, a second Self Barrier, or an incompatible protected-player death can expose the story.
cleric.posting: Answer TP during alignment claims. Give the full role and existing history when pressed or explaining protection; quiet nights need no invented dawn announcement.
willGuidance: Choose a plausible valuable recipient before night resolves; keep the number consistent with your actual observed visit.
Write Barrier 4, not saved 4, unless the actual feedback supports a save.
Use Self Barrier at most once. Do not promise a private protection plan to everyone.

Check the graveyard before posting: a dead target is a red flag, not automatic proof. An interrupted action or Unstoppable attack can explain death; an unblocked ordinary lethal attack conflicts with a genuine Barrier. Keep the original target rather than rewriting history.
cleric.blank:
Cleric
N1: Barrier [player] — [actual feedback, if any]
cleric.expanded: These are illustrative cover statements, not abilities the app performs. Low upkeep means less writing, not stronger evidence. Silencing your purported recipient still conflicts with a quiet protective story.

psychic.payoff: Creates immediate group leads, but requires a valid new vision and early posting each morning. Independent reports are more useful than lists assembled after everyone has claimed.
psychic.exposure: Parity, group sizes, the selected target, movement, and later revealed factions can contradict invented visions. Matching a visit supplies no real vision.
psychic.posting: Full-claim Psychic and post genuine visions near day start, normally D2 onward. Explain missing or failed visions rather than inventing replacement results.
willGuidance: Odd nights: Good vision with two names. Even nights: Evil vision with three names. Follow special client feedback in unusual late games.
Mark the player you selected and include them in that night’s vision.
A Good pair has at least one apparent good player; an Evil trio has at least one apparent evil player. Neither means exactly one.
Keep earlier visions visible and compare them with later evidence; do not silently replace names after claims or deaths.
psychic.expanded: Psychic trades daily work for visible contribution. Invented groups are not genuine results despite correct formatting. Cleric needs less upkeep, but neither unsupported story becomes confirmed.

sheriff.payoff: The result vocabulary is simple, and an independently posted check can focus discussion. Repeated Innocent entries are easy to write but provide limited independent credibility.
sheriff.exposure: Your visited target must match observer evidence. Suspicious is not available against every evil, and Innocent does not establish Town; frames and other effects matter.
sheriff.posting: Normally full-claim Sheriff with the exact result from D2 near the start of each day. Ask for an explanation of Suspicious without treating your accusation as unanswerable.
willGuidance: Use the literal Innocent or Suspicious feedback, keeping failed checks separate.
Choose an unresolved target and commit to that number before hearing everyone’s morning reports.
Record roleblock or another interruption instead of converting no result into Innocent.
Keep a reason for each target: a disputed claim or an unresolved vote is more useful than pretending silence proves evil.
sheriff.example:
Sheriff
N1: 4 — Innocent
N2: 7 — no result; roleblocked
sheriff.expanded: A fake Sheriff needs both a result story and a visiting story. Repeated Innocent results create little independent value; correctly reporting a framed target does not establish your faction.

investigator.payoff: Crime reports can create useful questions about action histories. The format is short, but explaining the distinction between Murder and Trespassing takes more care than a Sheriff entry.
investigator.exposure: Impossible crime claims on nonvisiting actions, wrong attack timing, or mismatched destinations weaken the story. Frames, Illusion, and Shroud also complicate real results.
investigator.posting: Full-claim Investigator with literal crime feedback early from D2; then ask the target for their action and relevant destinations. Separate the observed crime from your faction inference.
willGuidance: Use Murder, Trespassing, or No Crime as actually reported; preserve combined or unusual feedback verbatim.
Murder concerns an attack that night, not an old kill or a generic evil read.
Trespassing concerns opposing-faction visiting history, so Town can show it too; do not invent it for an action that never directly visits.
Log a failed investigation separately from No Crime and keep your selected target consistent.
investigator.example:
Investigator
N1: 4 — Trespassing
N2: 7 — No Crime
investigator.expanded: This cover needs a coherent crime and movement story. Neither No Crime nor crime-positive feedback establishes faction. Do not build an accusation around uncertain Jailor-execution interactions.

lookout.payoff: Can corroborate real visitors or expose contradictions directly. Strong apparent detail comes with a larger consistency burden than a one-target protective will.
lookout.exposure: Missing a known visible visitor, adding an impossible visitor, self-watching, or treating astral movement as ordinarily visible can expose a false account.
lookout.posting: Normally give useful observations from D2. If briefly withholding a list to compare independent claims, preserve the complete original result and explain the timing rather than inventing it afterward.
willGuidance: Write the watched house first, then who visited that house; this is the opposite direction from Tracker.
Use all visible visitors the game reports. No visible visitors is a real result; roleblocked is no result.
Do not normally watch yourself or claim that absence proves no astral action occurred.
Do not fill a list solely from morning claims and call it an independent discovery.
lookout.example:
Lookout
N1: Watch 4 — visitors 7, 9
N2: Watch 11 — no visible visitors
lookout.blank:
Lookout
N1: Watch [house] — [visible visitors / none / failed]
lookout.expanded: One verified visitor helps, but a fabricated complete list has many contradiction points. Partial knowledge from another ability must not be promoted into exhaustive Lookout observation.

tracker.payoff: Real destination information can verify an action account or expose a visiting contradiction. It is most convincing when recorded before the target announces where they went.
tracker.exposure: The target’s destinations and your own visit to the tracked player must both fit. No visible visit does not prove that the target did nothing.
tracker.posting: Normally full-claim Tracker with each result early from D2. Compare the tracked player’s own account without silently changing your destination list to match it.
willGuidance: Write tracked player -> their destinations, not the list of people who visited them.
Include multiple visible destinations when actually shown; corpse destinations remain valid references.
Use No visible visit only after a successful observation. Use failed or roleblocked for missing information.
If your information persists from an old ability, distinguish it from where you personally went tonight.
tracker.example:
Tracker
N1: 4 -> 9
N2: 7 -> no visible visit
tracker.blank:
Tracker
N1: [tracked player] -> [destinations / no visible visit / failed]
tracker.expanded: Real compatible tracking information helps. Guessing every destination is harder. Accurate information from persistent abilities still does not explain a contradictory personal visit on the current night.

seer.payoff: Friends/Enemies pairs can quickly organize a case, especially around an independently trusted anchor. The apparent payoff is high, but each pair commits to two players and a persistent target history.
seer.exposure: Reused or otherwise ineligible targets, an impossible pair result, or only one personal destination can expose the claim. Apparent faction effects can also distort genuine results.
seer.posting: Normally full-claim Seer and post each real pair result early from D2. Explain which other evidence makes one member a useful anchor; the result alone does not identify the evil member.
willGuidance: Use two distinct eligible players and retain a used-target history; follow the client’s reuse and revealed-target restrictions.
Show Friends or Enemies exactly. A failed pair is not a usable comparison.
Do not turn Enemies into both evil or Friends into confirmed Town.
Check whether your actual movement can support two personal visits before selecting this as a cover.
seer.blank:
Seer
N1: [eligible player] + [eligible player] — [Friends / Enemies / failed]
seer.expanded: Knowing two factions through another ability can help invent a result without reproducing two Seer visits. Extra actions or astral effects need specific explanations, not automatic guilt.

spy.payoff: Persistent Bugs can report distinctive effects over several nights and support later discoveries. That ongoing history gives value but creates more bookkeeping than a simple protective claim.
spy.exposure: Invented trigger roles, forgotten older Bugs, nonexistent visitor identities, and contradictory placement history are the main risks. A quiet night does not confirm the recipient.
spy.posting: Normally full-claim Spy from D2 and share real useful trigger information promptly. Keep placement nights separate from later trigger nights so Town can follow how you learned something.
willGuidance: Record each new Bug target and keep earlier Bugs in the active history.
Write the role or effect the feedback reports, not a visitor player number you were never given.
Label the trigger night explicitly, even when the Bug was placed several nights earlier.
No trigger and a failed Bug attempt are different outcomes; do not use either to clear a player.
spy.example:
Spy
N1: Bug 4 — no trigger
N2: Bug 7 — no trigger
spy.blank:
Spy
N1: Bug [player] — [actual feedback]
N[later]: Bug on [player] — [reported role/effect]
spy.expanded: Older Bugs create continuing obligations. Preserve literal feedback at uncertain interaction edges. A teammate’s real information still needs a plausible Bug history before it supports this cover.

coroner.payoff: Quiet before corpses exist, then durable killer records. Coven may know its book killer, but that supplies only part of the claimed process.
coroner.exposure: An ordinary N1 examination without an autopsy, invented killer roles, or ignoring accumulated records can expose the claim. Long stretches without actionable findings also create social pressure.
coroner.posting: Give the legal N1 limitation when asked, then publish useful day autopsies and night examination results as they become available. Do not pretend you had information before receiving it.
willGuidance: Write D2 autopsy separately from N2 examination; killer-role feedback arrives at night’s start.
Retain all previous autopsies because later examinations use the accumulated collection.
Use Match or No match within that collection; No match is not confirmed Town.
Preserve a failed examination as a failure and avoid invented framing excuses for results those effects do not alter.
coroner.example:
Coroner
N1: No autopsy available
D2: Autopsy 6 — killer role Poisoner
N2: Examine 9 — no match
coroner.blank:
Coroner
D[day]: Autopsy [corpse] — [killer role]
N[night]: Examine [player] — [match / no match / failed]
coroner.expanded: The example requires an actual corpse 6 killed by Poisoner. Killer-role transitions and Shroud need specific explanations. Empty autopsies delay verification pressure; they do not remove it.

bodyguard.payoff: One guard target per night makes routine recordkeeping simple. A real interception is meaningful, but a quiet protective history alone establishes little.
bodyguard.exposure: You promise interception of a direct harmful visitor and a counterattack. Fake saves, incompatible survivals, or more than two self-protections are harder to explain than quiet guards.
bodyguard.posting: Answer TP under alignment claims. Full-claim when protection coordination, a save, or a contradiction makes the exact ability relevant; keep unnecessary future targets private.
willGuidance: Write Guard and the selected player even when nothing was reported; choosing a target is not a save.
Use Self Protect at most twice and remember it supplies Basic Defense rather than a normal guard on another player.
Keep the destination aligned with any actual observed movement.
Do not erase a dead guard target automatically: astral bypass or additional attacks can explain some deaths; ordinary unblocked interception claims must still fit the evidence.
bodyguard.example:
Bodyguard
N1: Guard 4
N2: Self Protect — use 1
bodyguard.blank:
Bodyguard
N1: Guard [player] — [actual feedback, if any]
bodyguard.expanded: Low upkeep describes writing effort. Repeated alleged interceptions with no compatible harm or attacker evidence require explanation. A real Bodyguard can survive with suitable protection; survival alone is not disproof.

crusader.payoff: Can explain protection and a dangerous visitor outcome in one role. Routine entries are short, but visitors and death causes create more verification pressure than a quiet Cleric story.
crusader.exposure: You promise Powerful protection and an attack on one random direct visitor. An invented attacker identity, incompatible death label, or unsupported saved claim can unravel the account.
crusader.posting: Answer TP during alignment claims. Coordinate enough to reduce friendly visitor risk, and reveal Crusader when its dangerous protection explains an actual event or requires cooperation.
willGuidance: Write the fortified player, with protection feedback and visitor-attack feedback kept separate.
Do not claim to know which visitor was struck unless the game or independent evidence supplies it.
Record at most the actual visitor attack rather than pretending you hit every visitor.
Avoid promising to sit on a crowded TP/LO call without acknowledging the risk to friendly visitors.
crusader.example:
Crusader
N1: Fortify 4
N2: Fortify 7 — no attack feedback
crusader.expanded: A Jinx-like attack reproduces no Crusader protection. Quiet Fortify entries are not proof. Keep the preselected destination instead of choosing a convenient surviving house after dawn.

oracle.payoff: Role-based entries are short and astral movement can suit a genuinely nonvisiting role. That makes writing easy while genuine protection feedback remains difficult to reproduce.
oracle.exposure: You protect a role rather than visiting a numbered player. Repeated consecutive role choices, extra Oracle selections, or a visible direct visit can expose the story.
oracle.posting: Answer TP under alignment claims. Give exact role choices when the history is needed; do not describe a random numbered player as though you directly protected them.
willGuidance: Write Aegis Sheriff, for example, rather than Barrier 4.
Choose a different role on consecutive nights and use the Oracle self-role option only once.
If Grace Period disables N1 Aegis, write unavailable rather than a fictitious protection.
Do not claim a save just because a player with the chosen role survived; use actual feedback and avoid inventing their exact identity.
oracle.example:
Oracle
N1: Aegis Sheriff
N2: Aegis Seer
oracle.expanded: The example assumes N1 Aegis is enabled. A false Oracle supplies no actual protection. Later book attacks can break a formerly good astral movement fit.

trapper.payoff: Has a naturally quiet first night while building, then can offer protection and visitor-role feedback. The initial breathing room is useful, but the story needs a real state progression.
trapper.exposure: Placing before building, claiming a second active trap, or reporting impossible trigger information can expose the claim. A trap does not give a full list of player identities.
trapper.posting: Answer TP under alignment claims. Explain Build on the ordinary first night, then disclose placement or trigger history when relevant rather than implying the role checks someone immediately.
willGuidance: Start with N1 Build unless an actual setup effect changes availability.
Record placement on a later night and preserve that original house while the trap remains active.
If it triggers, copy reported roles and the actual protection outcome; do not invent visitor numbers.
Track triggered, dismantled, and rebuilt states separately so your next placement is legally timed.
trapper.example:
Trapper
N1: Build
N2: Place on 4
N3: Trap on 4 — no trigger reported
trapper.blank:
Trapper
N1: Build
N2: Place on [player]
N[later]: [trap state / actual trigger roles]
trapper.expanded: The example assumes building and placement succeeded. An active trap does not create a new nightly visit. Empty early entries delay verification pressure rather than eliminating it.

deputy.payoff: No nightly action list is needed, so writing is easy. That advantage is offset by a one-shot daytime ability other players may reasonably ask you to demonstrate.
deputy.exposure: You cannot reproduce a real Deputy shot through a different day ability. A reported private miss supplies little independent confirmation, and the single charge cannot be reused.
deputy.posting: Answer TK during alignment claims. Reveal the exact role when needed for a supported day-shot decision; do not shoot merely to stop people asking questions.
willGuidance: Write N1 No night ability rather than inventing a nightly check.
A shot is D2 or later and consumes your only use; record the day target and actual hit or miss.
Do not describe a private miss as a public demonstration of your identity.
After spending the shot, keep contributing with evidence and votes rather than adding imaginary night actions.
deputy.example:
Deputy
N1: No night ability
D2: Held shot — insufficient evidence
D3: Shot 9 — Miss
deputy.blank:
Deputy
D[day]: [held / shot player — actual outcome]
deputy.expanded: The sample is a possible chronology, not a recommended D3 shot. Misses can involve defense. Low typing comes with high demonstration pressure; a miss does not confirm either player.

trickster.payoff: Mirroring supplies a straightforward early protective story, and a genuine absorption yields an attacker role followed by a usable attack. That later evidence can be valuable.
trickster.exposure: Absorption has its own feedback and unlocks Unleash. Inventing an attack, mirroring while still holding it, or spending more than one Self Mirror can contradict the ability.
trickster.posting: Answer TK under alignment claims. Explain a real absorption or Unleash when it affects the case, while keeping unnecessary future offensive targets private.
willGuidance: Write the mirror target first; ordinary mirroring is not a kill and does not guarantee a save.
If an attack is absorbed, record the reported attacker role and hold that attack until Unleash.
Do not add another Mirror night while the stored attack remains unused.
Keep your one Self Mirror separate from ordinary mirrors and preserve failures instead of inventing an absorption.
trickster.example:
Trickster
N1: Mirror 4 — no absorption
N2: Mirror 7 — no absorption
trickster.blank:
Trickster
N1: Mirror [player] — [actual feedback]
N[later]: Unleash [stored role] on [player] — [outcome]
trickster.expanded: Quiet mirrors are easy to write. Real absorption feedback and later attack attribution are harder to reproduce. A genuine Unleash can endanger friendly visitors at the chosen house.

veteran.payoff: No target numbers are needed, and a real Alert can punish attackers. A quiet alert history is easy to record but offers little independent proof before compatible visitor outcomes exist.
veteran.exposure: Only three Alerts are available. A surviving direct visitor during an alleged Alert demands an explanation involving actual protection, interruption, or another relevant effect.
veteran.posting: Answer TK during alignment claims. Explain an Alert when it resolves visitor or death evidence; do not request protective visitors as a default way to manufacture confirmation.
willGuidance: Write Alert or No Alert for each night, tracking the three total uses.
Record only the visitor-shot count actually reported; a count does not reveal player identities.
If roleblocked or otherwise interrupted, preserve that fact rather than treating the selected Alert as successful.
Do not rewrite a quiet night to Alert only after learning someone claims a visit.
veteran.example:
Veteran
N1: No Alert
N2: Alert — no visitor shots reported
veteran.expanded: Low bookkeeping does not remove event-based verification. A genuine player should conserve Alerts when appropriate and avoid friendly casualties. A convenient invented Alert can conflict with independent visits.

vigilante.payoff: A legal loaded gun can remove a supported threat, and the will explains when an attack could occur. A fake claim can postpone a shot briefly but eventually faces ammunition and kill-evidence pressure.
vigilante.exposure: No N1 shot, shooting without loading, or simultaneous loading and shooting. Kill evidence and any Town-shot gun loss must fit the timeline.
vigilante.posting: Answer TK under alignment claims. Reveal exact shooting history when a death or contradiction makes it useful; avoid announcing an unsafe future shot just to seem active.
willGuidance: Start N1 Load if it succeeds; record an interruption instead if loading failed.
Keep Load and Shoot on separate nights and track at most three total loads.
A shot without a death is not a confirmed evil: defense or disruption can matter.
After the game reports a Town shot and removes the gun, stop claiming new loads or shots.
vigilante.example:
Vigilante
N1: Load — loaded
N2: Shoot 9 — target survived
N3: Load — loaded
vigilante.blank:
Vigilante
N1: Load — [outcome]
N2: [Load / Shoot player — actual outcome]
vigilante.expanded: The illustration assumes no Town-shot notification or lost gun. Different killing sources cannot freely substitute for Vigilante evidence. Holding remains mechanically possible but can grow socially weak.

admirer.payoff: An Obsession clue gives a search plan, and real Bestows can create a useful lasting effect. Credibility depends on more than listing one nightly destination.
admirer.exposure: Impossible Obsession categories, Care before discovery, unavailable Bestows, or obsolete marriage mechanics can expose the story. Others may ask for a real Bestow demonstration.
admirer.posting: Answer TS during alignment claims. Explain the clue and chronology when needed, and coordinate a genuine Bestow with a trusted useful player rather than broadcasting unnecessary private clues.
willGuidance: Record the starting Obsession subalignment and each Admire target with its actual result.
Use Care only after discovery, tracking its two charges separately.
Record daytime Bestows with a D label; they are not nighttime Admire actions, and only two are available.
Do not treat not-Obsession as a faction clear or fabricate an engagement or proposal.
admirer.example:
Admirer
Obsession clue: TP
N1: Admire 4 — not Obsession
D2: Bestow 7
admirer.blank:
Admirer
Clue: [subalignment]
N1: Admire [player] — [result]
D[day]: Bestow [player]
admirer.expanded: The example assumes a legal available Bestow. A false Admirer cannot supply its lasting effects. Keep discovery and reassignment history consistent rather than changing the Obsession after public claims.

amnesiac.payoff: Naturally has no N1 action before remembering, so the opening is simple. That grace period is temporary: the graveyard forces a concrete role transition and its future obligations.
amnesiac.exposure: Remaining unremembered despite an eligible transition, choosing an impossible role, or acquiring a public ability you cannot demonstrate weakens the story.
amnesiac.posting: Answer TS before remembering. Announce the genuine transition when necessary, retain the original Amnesiac history, and then follow the new role’s disclosure and result obligations.
willGuidance: Write Waiting to remember, not a night visit to select a corpse.
Remember is automatic at the eligible morning; Town Power priority and Unique-role restrictions can matter.
Mark the transition day and new role before logging its later actions.
Do not pretend hidden or altered graveyard art necessarily prevents genuine Remember from finding the true role.
amnesiac.example:
Amnesiac -> Sheriff
N1: Waiting to remember
D2: Remembered Sheriff
N2: 9 — Innocent
amnesiac.blank:
Amnesiac
D[day]: Remembered [actual role]
N[next]: [new-role action and feedback]
amnesiac.expanded: The example requires an eligible Sheriff death and actual transition. A fake claim must maintain both histories and may inherit demanding public-power obligations instead of an easy result role.

retributionist.payoff: No ordinary opening action is expected without a suitable corpse. Later, legal Town-corpse actions can provide genuine information or effects, especially for a role capable of reproducing them.
retributionist.exposure: Ineligible or Stoned corpses, impossible borrowed abilities, self-protection, and incorrect movement are major exposure points. Missing-corpse feedback is not a result.
retributionist.posting: Answer TS under alignment claims. Explain the empty graveyard initially, then give the corpse, destination, and useful borrowed feedback when a real action becomes available.
willGuidance: Write No usable corpse on ordinary N1 instead of inventing a visit.
List the dead player and their usable true role, followed by the living destination.
Your own visit goes to the corpse; the zombie goes to the living target. Keep that direction clear.
Track corpse contention and failures without inventing results; normal Town Retributionist cannot use Stoned corpses or protect itself.
retributionist.example:
Retributionist
N1: No usable corpse
N2: Sheriff 6 -> 9 — Innocent
retributionist.blank:
Retributionist
N[night]: [corpse and role] -> [living target] — [borrowed feedback / failed]
retributionist.expanded: The example requires an eligible dead Town Sheriff. Matching a legal borrowed action supports the story; unsuitable corpses or later book attacks can break that fit.

socialite.payoff: Can obstruct harmful visits and give a concrete rejected-visitor event. Maintaining the guest list and party sequence requires more work than simply writing a protection target.
socialite.exposure: Guests and affected visitors can compare effects. Repeated houses, too many invitations, incorrect immunity claims, or invented rejected identities create contradictions.
socialite.posting: Answer TS during alignment claims. Coordinate real trusted guests before blocking their visits, and reveal the relevant party history when an obstacle report needs explanation.
willGuidance: Keep daytime invitations separate from night parties: at most two manual guests total, one added per day.
Never ordinarily party at the same house on consecutive nights.
Write rejected someone only when the game reports it; that feedback does not identify who was rejected.
Party blocks incoming visits rather than roleblocking the resident; do not equate these different effects.
socialite.example:
Socialite
D2: Invite 7
N2: Party 4 — rejected someone
N3: Party 9 — no rejection reported
socialite.blank:
Socialite
D[day]: Invite [player]
N[night]: Party [house] — [actual feedback]
socialite.expanded: The sample omits N1 and assumes legal availability. Smog resembles only part of Party behavior. Guests and immunity differences can expose a false story even when destinations match.

tavern-keeper.payoff: A genuine Drink creates compatible roleblock feedback and can pressure an unresolved action. It is a stronger functional fit for a role that really Drinks than for a role merely making one visit.
tavern-keeper.exposure: Your target can report whether an effect occurred. Consecutive successful blocks through Hungover, incorrect messages, or a victim reporting Silence instead create problems.
tavern-keeper.posting: Answer TS during alignment claims. Give target history when asked and explain actual block feedback; a night without deaths does not establish that you stopped the killer.
willGuidance: Write Drink and the chosen target; do not describe every selected visit as a confirmed successful block.
After a successful Drink, rotate targets because Hungover prevents an immediate repeat block.
Separate failed or immune interactions from successful disruption.
Remember that visiting some killers is dangerous; a fake target story also needs to fit where you actually went.
tavern-keeper.example:
Tavern Keeper
N1: Drink 4
N2: Drink 7 — failed; Unknown Obstacle
tavern-keeper.blank:
Tavern Keeper
N1: Drink [player] — [actual feedback / failed]
tavern-keeper.expanded: A genuine block can support the story without proving Town allegiance. Do not relabel Silence as a roleblock or rewrite targets after hearing reports. Roleblock immunity does not bypass Party obstacles.

jailor.payoff: Real private jail conversations and executions create substantial evidence and control. A fake claim assumes a direct interaction that another player can readily confirm or deny.
jailor.exposure: A fabricated prisoner can dispute being jailed. Wrong timing, consecutive prisoners, an N1 execution, or incompatible execution outcomes expose the story quickly.
jailor.posting: Answer TPow when appropriate. Share real contradictions with Town, but avoid publishing an unnecessary future prisoner or treating a private recipient as trusted without evidence.
willGuidance: Choose the prisoner during the preceding day and record their exact claimed role and useful statements.
N1 permits questioning but not execution. Do not jail the same person consecutively.
Record released or executed explicitly and distinguish an attempted execution from its actual outcome.
Track the three executions and any loss of abilities; absence of night kills alone does not identify your prisoner as the killer.
jailor.example:
Jailor
N1: Jail 4 — claimed Cleric; released
N2: Jail 7 — claimed Sheriff; released
jailor.blank:
Jailor
N1: Jail [player] — claimed [role]; released
N[later]: [release / execution and actual outcome]
jailor.expanded: A well-written will cannot replace the private jail event. Execution should follow evidence, not demonstration pressure. Suitable protection and dangerous prisoners also complicate attempted execution outcomes.

marshal.payoff: No night targets or daily investigative results are required. A real Tribunal can change the voting day, but a fake claim cannot reproduce that conspicuous public action.
marshal.exposure: The role has two charges and one use per day. Inability to demonstrate a justified Tribunal is the central weakness of an otherwise easy will.
marshal.posting: Answer TPow during alignment claims. Announce and use Tribunal when a supported multi-target voting plan justifies it; claiming the role is not itself a reason to spend the ability.
willGuidance: Write No night ability instead of manufacturing nightly checks.
Use a D entry for a real Tribunal and list the people actually executed.
Do not label every Tribunal victim evil: execution is an event, not an alignment result.
Track charges and avoid claiming D1 use or repeated same-day uses.
marshal.example:
Marshal
N1: No night ability
D2: Held Tribunal — no supported multi-target case
D3: Tribunal — 4, 9 executed
marshal.blank:
Marshal
D[day]: [held / Tribunal — actual executed players]
marshal.expanded: The example lists two legal D3 executions, not confirmed evils or a required schedule. Minimal typing leaves severe public-demonstration pressure. Conversion can separate role demonstration from faction.

mayor.payoff: No nightly action history is needed. A real Reveal can create voting leverage, making the role easy to demonstrate when revealing is strategically worthwhile.
mayor.exposure: A false claimant cannot reproduce the public Reveal. A claimed vote-weight change must match the actual setup and day history rather than an invented night result.
mayor.posting: Answer TPow when asked for alignment. Reveal when the extra vote value and survival plan justify it; do not reveal solely because a will example contains a D2 line.
willGuidance: Write No night ability for quiet nights; Mayor does not investigate or visit a target.
Record Reveal on the actual day it happens, never D1 in the normal setup.
Keep observational vote notes distinct from ability results.
After revealing, continue recording useful cases and votes rather than inventing another activated power.
mayor.example:
Mayor
N1: No night ability
D2: Remained hidden
D3: Revealed
mayor.expanded: Minimal typing leaves immediate Reveal pressure. Extra votes do not make a suspicion correct. A demonstrated Mayor ability also does not establish allegiance where conversion or custom factions apply.

monarch.payoff: Knighting can produce a persistent visible voting effect and help trusted allies. Quiet holds are simple initially, but the promised Knights create later verification pressure.
monarch.exposure: You have two Knight uses and cannot invent the recipient’s actual Knight effect. Timing, dead or failed targets, and the living-Knight history must remain coherent.
monarch.posting: Answer TPow during alignment claims. Explain completed Knights when relevant, while remembering that the Knight effect proves an ability occurred rather than proving the recipient is Town.
willGuidance: Record each Knight attempt, its target, and whether the effect actually completed.
Do not mark a selection as completed before the night resolves.
Track the two charges from real outcomes; failed or dead-target attempts need the actual feedback.
Keep who is still a living Knight separate from the original list, and do not claim instant defensive benefits before resolution.
monarch.example:
Monarch
N1: Held Knight — no trusted recipient
N2: Knight 4 — completed D3
monarch.blank:
Monarch
N[night]: [held / Knight player — actual outcome]
monarch.expanded: The example illustrates conserving charges, not a mandatory N2 start. Recipients can verify Knight effects, while real Monarchs must assess allegiance before handing out permanent vote weight.

prosecutor.payoff: No night action or dawn result is expected. A real prosecution can resolve a supported daytime case, but a false claim has severe public-demonstration pressure.
prosecutor.exposure: The actual Prosecute event cannot be supplied by merely writing it. D1 use, use during Tribunal, too many charges, or incorrect aftermath conflicts with the role.
prosecutor.posting: Answer TPow under alignment claims. Use the ability only when the case justifies bypassing the normal vote, and explain the evidence rather than spending a charge to appear confirmed.
willGuidance: Write No night ability instead of an investigative or protective target.
Use D entries for prosecutions, with the actual target and outcome.
Track two total charges and at most one use per day; obey the live phase restrictions.
After a Town prosecution, preserve the actual penalty and remaining ability state rather than copying an outdated rule.
prosecutor.example:
Prosecutor
N1: No night ability
D2: Held Prosecute — insufficient evidence
D3: Prosecuted 9
prosecutor.blank:
Prosecutor
D[day]: [held / Prosecuted player — actual outcome]
prosecutor.expanded: The example does not identify player 9 as evil. A false claim cannot reproduce Prosecute. For the real role, a supported hold beats spending merely to demonstrate identity.

catalyst.payoff: Can enable extra actions on the recipient’s following ability cycle. A real coordinated effect can explain unusual action counts, but the setup and recipient-specific timing require care.
catalyst.exposure: The role must be legal in the deck, and a recipient can challenge whether Overcharge actually affected them. A promised effect on the wrong cycle or ability can undermine the claim.
catalyst.posting: Use Town Outlier when identifying alignment. Explain the application and expected cycle to a trusted recipient, then preserve the real feedback rather than promising every role works identically.
willGuidance: Record Overcharge target, actual application result, and the expected affected cycle.
Do not automatically claim a same-night extra action; follow that recipient’s ability and client feedback.
Keep observed extra actions separate from merely applying the charge.
Check setup eligibility and Unique-role conflicts before using this as a cover.
catalyst.example:
Catalyst
N1: Overcharge 4 — applied
D2: Asked 4 to confirm affected cycle
catalyst.blank:
Catalyst
N[night]: Overcharge [player] — [actual feedback]
Expected cycle: [confirmed timing]
catalyst.expanded: The sample intentionally avoids guessing recipient 4’s role or extra-action timing. A false Catalyst cannot supply the effect. Keep advanced timing conditional until the specific interaction is verified.

pilgrim.payoff: Has no ability or night-result burden, allowing a simple observation log. That same lack of an ability means the claim offers little independent verification.
pilgrim.exposure: The role must be allowed by the setup. An incompatible visible night visit or impossible slot story can contradict it, and an empty claim does not earn trust.
pilgrim.posting: Use Town Outlier when asked for alignment. Explain the legal role honestly and contribute concrete questions, vote reasoning, and comparisons rather than pretending to have a check.
willGuidance: Record public claims or vote changes with D labels; these are observations, not ability results.
Write No night ability instead of choosing a fictitious protective or investigative target.
Separate another player’s report from something you personally learned.
Keep the timeline stable so later contradictions are checkable, and verify that the deck can contain Pilgrim.
pilgrim.example:
Pilgrim
N1: No night ability
D2: 4 claimed TP; 7 changed claimed N1 target
pilgrim.blank:
Pilgrim
D[day]: [public observation and reason it matters]
pilgrim.expanded: This is low upkeep with weak independent verification. Real Pilgrims contribute through public reasoning. Visible visits or an excluded role slot can contradict a fake claim.
